one_liner: Rust minimal perfect hash with 8-bit pilots (PTHash descendant); queries 2.7-3.8x faster than BBHash, ~7.6x faster than CMPH CHD.
what_it_does: Builds a static function that maps a fixed set of n distinct keys (integers, strings or any `Hash` type) to unique indices in [0, n) using about 2.1-3.0 bits/key. It stores no keys, so it cannot reject non-members: a foreign key gets an arbitrary index. It is not a hash table. You build once from a slice (`<DefaultPtrHash>::new(&keys, PtrHashParams::default())`) and query with `index(&key)`, `index_batch::<K,_>` or the prefetching `index_stream::<32,_>`. Three type aliases pick the trade-off: `FastPtrHash` (non-minimal, returns values up to ~1.01n, 2.67 bits/key), `DefaultPtrHash` (minimal, 3.0 bits/key) and `CompactPtrHash` (multi-part with parallel build, 2.15 bits/key with Elias-Fano).
how_it_is_fast: It is a PTHash/PHOBIC-style bucket-placement MPHF. Keys hash into buckets, and each bucket stores a 'pilot' whose hash is XORed into the key hash to choose a slot. PtrHash limits pilots to 0..255 and stores them as a plain `Vec<u8>`, with no compact, dictionary or Elias-Fano decoding. When no pilot fits, construction uses cuckoo-style hash-and-evict. The result is that most queries cost one cache-line read plus a few multiply-high range reductions (Lemire's fastrange). With alpha=0.99, the ~1% of slots at or above n are remapped through a plain vector or CacheLineEF, which packs 44 Elias-Fano values into one cache line. `index_stream` hashes keys ahead and software-prefetches pilots 32 iterations early, which the paper shows saturates per-core memory bandwidth. Construction radix-sorts hashes and fills cache-sized parts.
when_to_use: Static key sets from ~1M to 10^9+ keys (the docs say it was tested up to 10^11) that are queried far more often than rebuilt, e.g. k-mer indexes, string-to-id dictionaries, or dense value arrays indexed by key.
Throughput-bound bulk lookups you can stream: on 1e9 integer keys, `index_stream` reaches 8.6-9.7 ns/key, vs 12.5-21.7 ns/key for a plain for-loop (SEA paper Table 1).
Tables much larger than L3, where cache misses dominate: the survey measured 1.0 L1 miss per query, vs 4.0-7.4 for BBHash and 11.4 for CHD.
You want fast construction without giving up query speed: 141 ns/key single-threaded at 2.99 bits/key (survey Table 6), or 27 ns/key on 6 threads (SEA Table 2).
Rust codebases, or C++ projects willing to link a Rust staticlib behind a small extern "C" shim, as MPHF-Experiments does.
when_not_to_use: Space is the priority: at 2.1-3.0 bits/key it is well above Consensus-RecSplit (1.58), SIMDRecSplit (1.81) and PHast (1.85-2.0) in survey Table 6.
You need membership tests or a mutable set: it has no insert/delete and no key storage. Any change means a full rebuild, and rejecting non-members needs a separate key or fingerprint array.

Pure C++ builds that cannot take a Rust toolchain. There is no C/C++ API. The only C++ port (bassiounix/PtrHash-cc, 3 stars) is an 'as is' rewrite for an LLVM libc RFC; its README says GPLv2 but GitHub detects no license file, and it has no benchmarks.

Small sets with the compact config: at 10,000 keys, survey Table 7 shows the cubic/EF config taking 44,300 ns/key to build (the linear/vec config takes 147 ns/key). The README warns that small inputs carry relatively large constant space overhead.
You need reproducible builds: construction is not deterministic (issue #36 is open; `build_part` uses an unseeded `fastrand::Rng`), so rebuilding the same keys reassigns indices.

integration.dependencies: bitvec, itertools, rand 0.10, rand_chacha, rayon, rdst (radix sort), fastrand, tempfile, mem_dbg, colored, log, fxhash, xxhash-rust, prefetch-index; default features add sucds (Elias-Fano) and cacheline-ef; optional: gxhash (StringHash), epserde (zero-copy/mmap serialization), extra hashers
integration.min_toolchain: Stable Rust. No MSRV is declared (crates.io rust_version is unset), but the rand 0.10 dependency needs Rust 1.85 (edition 2024). There is no C/C++ API.
integration.platforms: x86-64 and aarch64 are built and tested in CI. i686 and armv7 are cross-built only, with --no-default-features (sucds is 64-bit-only and gxhash needs AES). The repo's .cargo/config.toml sets target-cpu=native. Prefetch uses SSE on x86 or PRFM on aarch64 and is a no-op elsewhere. The paper's CacheLineEF lookup uses BMI2 PDEP, which it calls very slow on AMD Zen 2.
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. The built structure is immutable and queried through &self, so read-only sharing across threads is the natural model. Construction parallelizes internally with rayon.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: it fills the same keys-to-[0,n) MPHF role as BBHash, CHD or PTHash, but it is a Rust crate with its own API and serialization format (epserde), and C++ callers need an FFI layer

gotchas: `index_stream` returns an Iterator whose `next()` is `unimplemented!()`. Only fold-based consumers work (`sum`, `for_each`, `fold`); a plain `for` loop over it panics.

`new()` panics after 10 failed global seeds; use `try_new()` to get an `Option`. Duplicate keys always fail because duplicate hashes are rejected. `new_from_par_iter` discards the build result, so a failed build is not reported. Regular integer keys broke earlier FxHash-based versions (#19, #21): use `StrongerIntHash` for structured integers, and `StringHash128` for more than 10^9 string keys.

The paper's 'Default' config (lambda=3.5, cubic, CacheLineEF, 2.40 bits/key) is now `default_balanced()`, and the crate's `PtrHashParams::default()` is the paper's 'fast' config (~3.0 bits/key). Sharding requires SINGLE_PART=false (`CompactPtrHash`). Setting `params.sharding` on the default single-part types panics in `init`, and the repo's own examples/string_keys.rs does exactly that.

Before 2.1.0, safe `index()` could read past the remap array for a key outside the build set (#35). `Packed::index` impls still use `get_unchecked` inside safe fns, and epserde deserialization is `unsafe`. The maintainer says zero-copy CacheLineEF deserialization has alignment issues.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick PtrHash over PTHash when query latency and build speed matter and Rust is acceptable: 45 vs 76 ns/query and 141 vs 516 ns/key build in survey Table 6, or 37 vs 77 ns in SEA Table 2. Prefer PHast/PHast+ (also Rust) for slightly faster queries at ~2 bits/key (38-44 ns, 1.85-2.07 bits/key), and SIMDRecSplit or Consensus-RecSplit when getting below 2 bits/key justifies 5x+ slower queries.
verified_claims_summary: The survey (arXiv 2506.06536v3, Table 6) linked ptr_hash 1.1.0 as a Rust staticlib (Rust 1.85, target-cpu=native) and ran it against C++ BBHash and CMPH CHD (GCC 14.2, -O3 -march=native). The run used 100M random 10-50-byte strings, single-threaded, on an i7-11700 pinned at 2.5 GHz. PtrHash queried in 45-47 ns vs 127-173 ns for BBHash and 356 ns for CHD, and built in 141-358 ns/key vs 157-273 and 1,522 ns/key. The author's SEA 2025 paper (300M strings, 6 threads, i7-10750H at 2.6 GHz, compiler not stated) reports 37 ns (23 ns streaming) vs 77 ns for the fastest PTHash config; no source compares against std::unordered_map.
status_note: Actively maintained by a responsive single author: v2.1.1 shipped 2026-08-27 and the last commit is 2026-08-28. It is MIT-licensed with ~62k crates.io downloads. The 1.x to 2.x break changed type aliases and parameter names and invalidated old on-disk structures, and the benchmarked 1.1.0 predates 2.x. Issue #40 reports 2.x's default_compact building 1.6-1.9x slower at 1M keys because it uses fewer parts.
